parsed.explanation: The unit responds to a clearly visible, medium-sized wheel of a road vehicle sitting inside its wheel arch, seen from the side or at an angle, with a preference for the front wheel. The vehicle type does not matter much.
parsed.evidence: Clearly visible wheels give d +1.38 and medium-sized wheel-plus-arch gives d +1.10, both at percentile 100, while small or hidden wheels, front/rear views and photos with no wheel are strongly negative (percentile 0). parsed.missing_data: Activations on wheel arches without tires, and on isolated tires or bicycle wheels outside vehicle classes, to tell whether the arch, the tire or their combination drives the unit.

real_s2.explanation: The unit responds to a clearly visible road-vehicle wheel sitting in its wheel arch, seen from the side or a three-quarter angle at medium scale, and it fires most for the front wheel. It responds weakly or not at all when the wheel is small, hidden, seen head-on, or has no arch around it.

parsed.explanation: The unit responds to a clearly visible road-vehicle wheel sitting in its wheel arch, seen from the side or a three-quarter angle at medium scale, and it fires most for the front wheel. It responds weakly or not at all when the wheel is small, hidden, seen head-on, or has no arch around it.
parsed.evidence: Whether the wheel is clearly visible has the strongest effect (d +1.38 vs -1.10 for small or partly hidden wheels, percentile 100), and wheels inside an arch (+0.86) beat wheels without one (-0.29). Angled views (+0.67) are as strong as or stronger than pure side views (+0.28), front/rear views are negative (-1.09), medium size is best (+1.10) while far-away wheels are negative (-0.97), and orientation was never tested because every photo was upright.
parsed.missing_data: Photos of tilted or rotated vehicles to test the 'upright' claim, and isolated tires or arches on their own to see which part drives the response.

parsed.explanation: The unit responds to a clearly visible road-vehicle wheel sitting inside its wheel arch or fender, seen at medium scale from a side or three-quarter angle, especially the front wheel of vans, buses and trucks.
parsed.evidence: Within classes, clearly visible vehicle wheels give d +1.38 while small or partly hidden wheels give -1.10 (both extreme percentiles), and medium-sized wheel-plus-arch gives +1.10 against -0.97 for small ones; front or rear views (-1.09) and wheels without an arch (-0.29) score lower. parsed.missing_data: Rotated or overturned vehicles to test orientation, close-up crops of isolated wheel arches without a wheel (and wheels without arches) outside vehicle classes, and non-vehicle round objects inside arch-like shapes.

null_s2.explanation: The unit responds to a clearly visible, round vehicle wheel seen from the side, most often a front wheel; it does not need the surrounding wheel arch.

parsed.explanation: The unit responds to a clearly visible, round vehicle wheel seen from the side, most often a front wheel; it does not need the surrounding wheel arch.
parsed.evidence: Activity is higher for clearly visible wheels (d +0.35) and side-view round wheels (d +0.36, percentile 96), and much lower for front/rear narrow views (d -0.84, percentile 1), partly hidden wheels (d -0.60) and rear wheels (d -0.60). Whether an arch is visible makes no difference (separation percentile 54), and the 9 no-wheel photos are oddly high (d +0.42), which hints that other round shapes may also drive it.
parsed.missing_data: Out-of-class photos with round non-wheel objects (and wheels without arches, or rotated or tilted vehicles) would show whether it is wheel-specific or a general circle detector.

parsed.evidence: Viewing angle separates activity unusually well (percentile 99): round side-view wheels are positive (d +0.36), while narrow front/rear-view wheels (d -0.84) and small or partly hidden wheels (d -0.60) are among the most negative in the layer.
